305.history: A scatter of grey houses above a shingle beach where the coast turns, its nets strung to dry on frames mended every spring with the fathers' twine. It kept one of Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh on the capes, whose keeper wrote on the first morning of the age that no ship came. Its small church in a net-store answered to the same distant bishops as the great one at Cnoc ghorm. In the ninth year the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane kept Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise in the open on the headland below the old light, as no keeper had kept it before; the bishops called it irregular in a letter that stayed folded behind the altar-cloth. The magistrate fined her for it in the twenty-seventh year, Tional nan Tuathach paid the fine, and the vigil went into a lent byre. In the seventeenth year the town's light was given a Dia-thìreach keeper under a warrant bidding him report what he saw by land as well as by sea, and in the thirty-second year he reported the vigil kept silent in the tower's shadow; the council answered nothing.
305.known_for: Oidhche Glaise on the headland, and the fifth light

142.history: A market town of the northern coast, nearer the shire's seat than Baile chrom and twelve miles from it. In the ninth year the north raised here the largest church it had built since the crossing closed, its stone hauled from a quarry two shires south on carts Tional nan Tuathach paid for by subscription, and in its tower hung the bell of the old chapel at Ros bheag, crated in a barn since the first spring; it rang first on a market morning and carried to the shore road. The next year the church opened a school for its priests, with a master from Seann Skell. A thin blessing of the boats was kept here each spring, and after Seann Bhral refused the north in the twenty-fifth year Mary Coyle made it the full Fleadh na Mara: more than fifty boats came on the second Sunday of an Gearran in the twenty-sixth year, blessed with heather dipped in harbour water, and David Hale counted them. Rathad nan Cairtearan runs through it south to Àth fhada.
142.known_for: the church of the Ros bheag bell, and Fleadh na Mara

160.history: The mill-town the humans built to watch the northern landing and left to whoever wanted the keeping of it. In the ninth year it was granted a market right for the inland country of the north-west, the second such right any northern town had been given, and the carpenters spent most of a month laying hurdles on the old common green, where mill hands had played ball, to pen the first market's beasts. The Tuathaich drovers of the hill farms, who had walked their stock the long way south, brought them here on set days instead, and from here the droves went on south by the old tracks to Ceann leathan; by midsummer the green stood full every market day and the innkeepers let every room. The vigil-keepers of Oidhche Glaise answered to nobody south of it, and carters driving in from it heard the Cnoc ghorm bell before they saw the tower.

279.history: A village on the eastern road where the walkers to the holy well of Allt an Àigh lodge on their way. In the tenth year it was raising a long hall for them, and in the eleventh the hall stood; its keeper, an old woman, wrote each walker's name and shire in a cracked-spined ledger, which held travellers from better than twenty shires that first summer and from fifty by the end of the decade, north and south and east and west of the island together on the one road. The under-clerk Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill lodged here a night with her mother, of an Old Spirits house, on their walk to the well in the tenth year, and thought of the ledger growing a name longer every year while the wall the council had talked of went undrawn. The cairn at the well itself, the keeper told them, grows a little taller every year.
279.known_for: the walkers' hall and its ledger

135.history: The pit town under An Sloc Mòr, at the head of Slighe a' Ghuail. The line was mended through to its pithead in the twelfth year, and the first train out of it had its blessing said over the coal in the first wagon, the old custodian from Muileann dhearg being unwilling to walk the footplate. A quarry was cut above it in the thirteenth year and its dressed stone went south under the Mac Ùisdein wave-mark. Comann nan Gualadairean was chartered in the yard before its pithead on a cold day of an t-Samhain in the thirteenth year, each Dia-thìreach hewer swearing on a lump of coal, its Tuathaich families kept at their work. The guild bound sixty apprentices in its hall after the fall at Muileann dhearg, none of them Tuathaich, and forty households left for the ports that autumn. In the sixty-first year its lowest galleries lay eleven fathoms under water and its three great pumps went south by rail to Seann Bhral's new dry dock.
135.known_for: An Sloc Mòr's pithead, the hewers' oath, and the pumps

491.history: A town of narrow streets and spoil-stone chapels five miles from the great shaft, grown fat on An Sloc Mòr's overflow and working its own pits to keep the greater mine's yield steady. It took the most of the hungry families who came to the vein in the twelfth year, and its old druid hall was cut into lodgings over ground the Board had to mark as sound or not. Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's house here sent the old custodian who blessed the first train. It sent the largest company to the first Còmhrag. The Cill ghlas district under it, shut since Scàineadh Cill ghlas of the humans' time, was reopened by the Board; on the first day of an t-Iuchar in the thirty-ninth year its galleries fell and thirty-one men died, and they were buried in a single ground at the edge of the town's yard, the custodian reading over each grave. By the fifty-seventh year its maor counted above sixty houses empty; its Fèidh hall, given back to Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, was locked by its last teacher, and its bell sold to Caol shean.

354.history: The shunting town where the line from An Sloc Mòr meets the older line down to the ports. The council mended Slighe a' Ghuail as far as it in the eighth year and no further, and the humans' own timetable, copied fair, was hung on a board at its terminus. Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn laid new sidings here in the thirteenth year, and the shunting families, who had worked the humans' small engines, were counted apart on a roll of their own and housed in the rows nearest the lines; in the twenty-fourth year the rows had more children born than they had cradles for, among them Seachran and Brean. Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer of the town, won the first Còmhrag. In the sixty-third year its yard families stopped the coal trains three days over a cut wage, with Dòmhnall Ruadh mac Ailein as their spokesman; the wage was restored and eleven men dismissed.
354.known_for: the shunting rows and the stopped trains

88.history: A town on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, seat of custodian houses of the east. Its ship-chandlers took a guild charter in the fourteenth year and with it the sole right to fit out An Crùn's patrol boats, and the yearly fitting-out became the guild's show of its charter before the shire's maor. Seumas mac Coinnich Ghlais, who sat for the eastern custodian houses at the council's table, was a man of the town, and it was he who brought a map to the council in the tenth year and proposed the border wall, and saw it die without a vote. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's mother lived in a village by it, and the two parted here on the eastern road after the walk to Allt an Àigh. A room over a chandler's shop here was the last of the eleven northern schools Tional nan Tuathach counted in the twenty-ninth year.
88.known_for: the chandlers and the patrol boats

137.history: The lamp-making town of the vein country, whose forges turned out the greater part of every shaft-lamp the pits burned. Its lamp-makers were chartered as a guild in the fourteenth year, and set their mark, a flame struck over a hammer, on every lamp that left their sheds, so that the lamp carried the record of where it was made and under what oath; of all the guild marks the humans' traders had copied this one only. The carters of Slighe a' Ghuail complained at every siding between it and Muileann chaol when, in the sixty-second year, the lamp-makers halved their making for want of coal to fire their forges, the coal reaching the town thinner and dearer each season. Shaft-lamps were lent from pit to pit after that, and Comann nan Gualadairean kept a minute-book of who lent to whom.

106.history: A weaving town of the south whose weavers took a guild charter in the fifteenth year: the council's clerks cut them a seal of a shuttle over a fleece and entered the grant in a calf-bound book at Cathair dhearg after a fee and a feast, and the guild barred any weaver who had not served seven years under a master. Its pipers played for coin at the first fair at Muileann òg, and its cloth came to that fair from its looms. A drought at the town went into Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd in the twenty-eighth year beside Brìghde's death. Its maor petitioned in the thirty-eighth year that Doire chaol, five miles off, had outgrown being governed at second hand, and the new shire was cut from his, the only shire cut new since the drawing; he sent its first dues south with a note wishing its maor better luck. In the fifty-fifth year its weavers began a grey thread of their own in the selvedge of their finer bolts. A teacher from the town kept the smallest of Cnoc leathan's six schools.
106.known_for: the weavers' seal, and the cutting of Doire chaol

234.history: A weaving town of the northern moss, close enough across the moor from Doire ghlas that a boy could walk it before the school bell finished. Its householders came to the first sitting of Tional nan Tuathach. Daniel Frayne was a fisherman's son of the town and walked from it daily to Agnes Pike's byre in the fifteenth year; he kept a bindery here from the forty-eighth year on a mended cider-press, teaching young Tuathaich hands a craft the southern guilds would not, and bound Tional nan Tuathach's registers and Muileann shean's primers at his bench. The wool trains of the forty-first year set out from it for Muileann òg by Rathad nan Cairtearan. Clàr nan Leòn was bound here, and its second copy kept at a house in the town that no southern search ever troubled. Frayne, the town's bookbinder and by then Tional nan Tuathach's speaker, carried the Doire ghlas mill's ledgers and Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's refusal to Seann Bhral in the fifty-ninth year and brought home the ruling.

44.history: The town where Rathad na Mèinne from the central mountains comes down to the Abhainn uaine above the gulf. It grew a different way from the pit towns in the twelfth year, taking in carters, inns and a ropewalk, doubling its people within a decade and being given a shire court. Its carters carried the news of the coast south; it was from a carter of the town that Iain Mapa first heard of the raiders off Cathair gheal, third-hand and late. A quarryman of the town put Calum Ruadh down twice in the first hour of the first Còmhrag, and stood over him laughing the second time.

204.history: A town of the south-west, seat of houses of Òrd na Cloiche, whose Clach is the Lia Fàil and not Crom's stone. In the seventh year its houses were bidden to send witnesses to the settling of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail at Seann Skell; they sent none, and a letter wishing Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail well and promising nothing further, which Dòmhnall mac Thormoid copied onto the first page of his ledger of letters. Òrd na Cloiche kept its own houses, its own mark cut plain over its doors, and its own dealings through the age: it lent coin against a town's dues where a town's need outran a maor's patience, and its paper stood for coin at Inis thais until the coin came.

246.history: A town east of the mountain, where the town's own custodians had kept rolls and bound books since before An Dealachadh on planks above standing water in a cellar under the old grain-store. In the sixteenth year the council founded an Leabharlann here and named Ailean mac Iain, Ailean Leabhar, its first keeper; the council's minute-books and the humans' tithe ledgers came east to it, the copyists turned its dates into the civil calendar, and its keepers opened Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean, Leabhar nan Aithrisean and Clàr nan Aoisean, counting An Aois Ailein apart. Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd kept her seat here from the eighteenth year rather than at the capital. The town was given a market charter in the seventeenth year, its first fair held in an Leabharlann's yard. Ailean was buried in a small ground behind an Leabharlann in the fortieth year, and Mòrag nic Coinnich kept it thirty years after, calling in the shire chests and building the new wing with its empty fourth floor. A chur san Leabharlann, to put it in an Leabharlann, was first said here.

276.history: A village a few miles from an Leabharlann, on the stream below it. In the eighteenth year a family of millers who had not grain enough to keep three wheels busy built a paper-mill here instead, and an Leabharlann's copyists spoke of its first sheets before they had them in hand. Forty quires of its paper went up to Muileann chaol on a borrowed cart, better and cheaper, the copyists judged, than anything the council's stationers had sent, and within the year near enough every sheet an Leabharlann used came from the one stream; nearly every page of Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd in this age is written on its paper. The road east past it smells of wet paper before the mill comes in sight.

62.history: A parish of the island's north-east, whose Seann Spioradan house keeps a parish roll that names its households back before the coming of the humans, older than any book the south's forty chests gave up to the first chronicle circuit. In the nineteenth year the old keeper heard the circuit clerks' warrant once, without asking it twice, and let the roll be copied at his own table under his own eye, but would not let the book travel so much as to the harbour, telling them a book kept that many generations belonged to the house and not to any seal. The copy went to Muileann chaol; the book stayed.
62.known_for: the parish roll copied and not carried

38.history: A Tuathaich fishing harbour of the north coast. On the second night of an t-Sultain in the nineteenth year a westerly drowned eleven men of seven of its boats, Thomas Coyle of Caol mhòr among them; the sea gave back two broken hulls and a stranger's oar. The town had no lifeboat. Mary Coyle wrote the eleven names on one sheet for the mason in the order the boats went out, and Tional nan Tuathach opened a subscription the same week; the lifeboat, white-painted with cork along her gunwales, came up the coast from Cuan shean in an Cèitean of the twentieth year and was put into the water off the town's jetty by that autumn's five widows. Its boats sailed with Mary Coyle to Seann Bhral in the twenty-fifth year, and its fishermen walked to Walter Hale's burial.
38.known_for: the eleven drowned, and the lifeboat

476.history: A walled town of the north-west coast, its harbour a shallow bay below the town wall. In the second year its people loosed the humans' locked loft of nets to every boat in the harbour on a single tide. From the twelfth year ships flying no flag worked its waters; a fishing house was burned below the town and two boats taken, and the council's minute asked that the matter be watched. In the twentieth year Nell Barrow, a skipper's widow, wrote twice to the council for a boat or leave to arm its own and was answered by neither letter. On the night of 8 an Giblean three flagless hulls stood into the bay; the largest ran onto a shifted bar and was boarded and burned by seven town boats before dawn, at a cost of two dead and four hurt. The council fined the town four purses of Bonn na Rìoghachd for bearing arms without leave, and Walter Hale carried Tional nan Tuathach's share of it north; the fine was counted out at the maor's door.
476.known_for: the bay cleared, and the fine paid

23.history: The mountain town of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein, whose family had held an overseer's post under the humans at An Sloc Mòr. Uisdean mac Ùisdein came from it to the capital in the eleventh year to take Cead an t-Sluic Mhòir, and in the twentieth year the house raised a market cross at its own cost, cut on all four faces with its name, and moved the wool and coal markets to its foot. Comhairle nam Mèinnean moved its clerks here in the twenty-seventh year, into rooms above the wool market, and set down that its surveys should be kept in its own presses and not sent to an Leabharlann. The house built its stone hall of spoil-stone in the thirtieth year and feasted Comann nan Gualadairean in it. After Sireadh na Dàrna Fèithe the house let the hall to the Board in the fifty-second year, and Catrìona nic Neacail hung her one sheet of the vein on its chamber wall in the fifty-sixth.
23.known_for: Taigh Mhic Ùisdein, and the Board's presses
